about: Side topic X4 (How are energy rules made?): how U.S. energy rules start from a law and follow separate tracks (a regulator's rules and tariffs, a rate case, a permit), with one finished federal rulemaking (FERC Order No. 2222, issued 17 September 2020) and Kansas's commission (the KCC) as the state example. Every fact is from a dated primary source below; no live proceeding is described. Prairie Town's utility and its project are fictional and illustrative.
project: Prairie Town's utility (fictional), in Kansas, wants a wind farm and a new 345 kV line (kV, kilovolts: the line's voltage) about 40 miles long, and to recover their cost in its rates.

root.title: Law
root.text: Congress or a state legislature gives a regulator its authority.

tracks.title: Market rules and tariffs
tracks.text: FERC writes rules for wholesale markets and transmission; an RTO or a utility files its tariff at FERC.

tracks.title: Retail rates
tracks.text: The state commission, in Kansas the KCC, decides each utility's rate case.

tracks.title: Project permits
tracks.text: A county, the state or a federal agency, depending on what is built and where.

chain.note: These approvals follow separate tracks and can overlap: one project may need a tariff change, a rate decision and permits at the same time.

hook.q: How long did one federal rule take

steps.label: A panel at FERC's open meeting
steps.text: FERC opens its inquiry with a panel on electric storage at a public open meeting.

steps.label: Data requests and a request for comments
steps.text: Staff ask the six RTOs and ISOs for their rules and invite comments; 44 arrive.

steps.label: A proposed rule
steps.text: FERC proposes the rule in a notice of proposed rulemaking; 109 comments follow.

steps.label: A technical conference
steps.text: More than 50 people and organizations speak over two days; 52 comments follow.

steps.label: The final rule, Order No. 2222
steps.text: FERC issues the final rule; it takes effect 60 days after it appears in the Federal Register.

steps.label: Each RTO files its tariff changes
steps.text: Each RTO or ISO must file the tariff changes within 270 days of the rule's publication.

rateCase.label: Application
rateCase.text: The utility files an application with supporting data; it needs the commission's approval to change rates.

rateCase.label: Staff review
rateCase.text: Staff examine the utility's books and records, ask for more data and recommend; the recommendation is not binding.

rateCase.label: Testimony
rateCase.who: The utility, staff, CURB and other intervenors
rateCase.text: Expert witnesses file written testimony; the Citizens Utility Ratepayer Board (CURB) speaks for homes and small businesses, and other [[intervenor|intervenors]] may join.

rateCase.label: Public hearing
rateCase.text: Not required by law, but generally held in significant cases; public comments become part of the record.

rateCase.label: Evidentiary hearing
rateCase.who: The three commissioners and every party
rateCase.text: When held, this [[evidentiary-hearing|evidentiary hearing]] presents the facts formally; commissioners review testimony and exhibits and may question witnesses.

rateCase.label: Order
rateCase.text: In most cases the commission issues its decision, a written order, within 240 days of the filing; the limit can be waived in certain circumstances.

settlement.q: The utility, the commission's staff and CURB sign a settlement. Must the commission accept it

options.label: No, it may accept, reject or change it

feedback.yes: No: the KCC says it does not have to accept a proposed settlement.
feedback.no: Right: the KCC may accept, reject or modify a settlement; the commissioners decide.

cards.text: Rules letting small resources join SPP's wholesale markets as a group
cards.why: Federal: FERC's Order No. 2222 sets them, and SPP files its tariff with FERC.

cards.text: The price per kWh a Prairie Town home pays its investor-owned utility
cards.why: State: the KCC sets and regulates the rates of the utilities it oversees.

cards.text: A siting permit for the new 345 kV line, about 40 miles long
cards.why: State: in Kansas a line of 230 kV or more and at least 5 miles long needs the KCC's siting permit.

cards.text: Approval of where the wind farm's turbines may stand
cards.why: Local, in most places: the county, sometimes with state regulators; a few states decide alone.

cards.text: A check that the tall turbines are safe for aircraft
cards.why: Federal: the Federal Aviation Administration reviews tall structures for airspace obstruction.

cards.text: Mandatory reliability standards for the bulk power grid
cards.why: Federal: FERC certified NERC in 2006 to write them, and they are mandatory and enforceable.

cards.text: A permit to put solar panels on a Prairie Town roof
cards.why: Local: the city or county permit office issues it.

voice.q: Which can any member of the public do

options.label: Comment on a KCC rate case
Comment on a FERC proposed rule
Vote on the commission's final order

feedback.kcc: Yes, and more: the public can also comment on a FERC proposed rule.
feedback.ferc: Yes, and more: KCC rate cases take public comments too.
feedback.both: Right: KCC comments enter the case record, and FERC took 109 comments on the proposed rule behind Order No. 2222.
feedback.vote: No: the commissioners decide; the public comments, and parties who intervene file testimony.

facts.what: How long the KCC has, in most cases, to decide a rate case after the filing date; the limit can be waived in certain circumstances.
From FERC's first open-meeting panel (19 November 2015) to Order No. 2222 (17 September 2020): 4 years, 9 months and 29 days.
Comments FERC received on its proposed rule of 17 November 2016.
KCC commissioners, appointed by the Governor to overlapping four-year terms; no more than two of one party.
In Kansas, a line this large or larger needs a KCC siting permit: a public hearing within 90 days of the filing and a final order within 180 days.

stop.title: This side topic stops at how rules are made
stop.lede: Rules enter the course as who decides what, in what order and when; reading legal texts and following live cases is the work of lawyers and regulatory staff.
includes: Who makes which rule: Congress and FERC, a state legislature and its commission, counties and cities.
How a law leads, on separate tracks, to market rules and tariffs, retail rates and permits, and where the public can take part.
Reading dates: one finished federal rulemaking and a state commission's rate-case clock.
leaves: Legal texts, their interpretation and legal advice.
Live proceedings: today's open dockets and pending rules.
Other states' and other countries' procedures, which differ.

ferc-primer.cite: FERC staff, Energy Primer: A Handbook of Energy Market Basics, p. vi and p. 35
used: FERC's authority comes from the Natural Gas Act, the Federal Power Act and the Interstate Commerce Act (p. vi).
State regulators approve retail rates, largely cost-of-service, and utilities' investments in generation and distribution (p. 35).
FERC certified NERC in 2006, and reliability standards became mandatory and enforceable (p. 35).

ferc-2222.cite: FERC, Order No. 2222, Participation of Distributed Energy Resource Aggregations in Markets Operated by Regional Transmission Organizations and Independent System Operators, Docket RM18-9-000, final rule
used: Effective 60 days after publication in the Federal Register; tariff changes due within 270 days of publication (cover page).
The procedural history from which the six milestones are selected, with the comment counts (pp. 10-12).

kcc-role.cite: Kansas Corporation Commission, The Commission's Role
used: Authority from K.S.A. 74-601 to 74-631; the present commission established by the Legislature in 1933.
Three members appointed by the Governor to overlapping four-year terms, no more than two of the same party.
The Utilities Division establishes and regulates rates; most electric cooperatives and municipalities are not regulated by the KCC.

kcc-rates.cite: Kansas Corporation Commission, How rates are set
used: Two steps: the revenue requirement (approved expenses, including depreciation and income taxes, plus a return on the rate base), then rate design.
The utility files an application; in most cases 240 days from the filing date for the KCC's decision, a written order; the limit is waivable.
Staff review and a non-binding recommendation; the Citizens Utility Ratepayer Board (CURB) and other intervenors; expert testimony.
A public hearing, generally held in significant cases; an evidentiary hearing; the commission may accept, reject or modify a settlement.
Public comments received during the comment period are entered into the official case record; comment online, by mail or by phone, citing the docket number.

ks-siting.cite: Kansas Statutes, K.S.A. 66-1,177 and K.S.A. 66-1,178, as amended by House Bill 2040 (Kansas Register, 17 April 2025); cited by name, without a link
used: K.S.A. 66-1,177: an electric transmission line is at least 5 miles long and used for the bulk transfer of 230 kV or more.
K.S.A. 66-1,178: a KCC siting permit before site preparation or construction; a public hearing within 90 days of the filing, in a county the line crosses.
K.S.A. 66-1,178 as amended in 2025: a final order within 180 days of the filing.

doe-wind-guide.cite: U.S. Department of Energy, WINDExchange, Land-Based Wind Energy Economic Development Guide, Regulatory Considerations
used: The primary siting authority is the local government, or the local government with state regulators; only four states give it to the state alone.
Federal Aviation Administration approval may be needed for airspace obstruction.

doe-solarapp.cite: U.S. Department of Energy, 160 Communities Now Automating Solar Permitting with SolarAPP+
used: Local jurisdictions issue the permits for residential rooftop solar.
